tier_reason: Leopard's Benchmarks.md lists WH256 encode 661.644 MB/s and decode 830.103 MB/s against CM256 99.6658/104.651 MBps and Longhair 100.342/96.3757 MB/s exactly as claimed, but these are first-party numbers ('not being very rigorous') on an unnamed AVX2 laptop with no compiler or flags, and the benchmarked catid/wh256 code now returns 404, so the run is not reproducible.

corrections.caveats: First-party numbers from the same author as CM256, 'not being very rigorous' on one laptop, with no CPU model, compiler or flags, and one configuration (k=m=128, 64 KB pieces). The measured code is catid/wh256, a pre-production GF256 branch; github.com/catid/wh256 now returns 404, so the benchmarked code is not public (current Wirehair 2 is described as a pure-GF(256) API, but its equivalence to WH256 is not shown). The numbers sit in the Leopard repo, not Wirehair's. The comparison covers only the author's own codecs; in the same table the author's Leopard encodes faster (1964.98 MB/s vs 661.644 MB/s), so Wirehair is fastest only at decode. Reed-Solomon (MDS, practical only up to 255 pieces) and a fountain code (about 0.025 extra blocks of overhead on average) are not like-for-like. Baseline is the author's own CM256 rather than Jerasure, ISA-L or Zfec, and the author notes CM256's inner loops could still be improved with GF256. Wirehair's own README benchmarks only compare Wirehair 1 with Wirehair 2 (GCC 13.3, AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 9985WX, per docs/benchmarks/README.md) and show WH2 slower at 64-byte blocks, so they are no evidence against an outside baseline. Category erasure-codes is not one of the wave categories; filed under compression-and-encoding as the nearest domain.

notes: Numbers and derived 6.6x encode / 7.9x decode ratios check out against the page. Shortcomings: first-party, unnamed laptop CPU, no compiler/flags, baseline is the author's own CM256, benchmarked wh256 repo is gone (404), and the author's Leopard beats WH256 at encode in the same table. Metadata (BSD-3-Clause, 394 stars, last commit 2026-09-17, not fork/archived) confirmed.

tier_reason: Independent third-party benchmark with public code (JacksonAllan/c_cpp_hash_tables_benchmark main.cpp plus shims/ and blueprints/), compiler GCC 13.2.0 via MinGW-w64, flags -O3 -DNDEBUG (README: g++ -I. -std=c++20 -static -O3 -DNDEBUG -Wall -Wpedantic main.cpp) and CPU AMD Ryzen 7 5800H all stated; heatmap values for std and uthash match the record exactly.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Article text: "uthash's iteration is about twice as fast as std::unordered_map's iteration (albeit still extremely slow)". Heatmap for 0-20M keys (total time relative to the fastest table, std::unordered_map vs uthash): iterate 87.83 vs 37.39 (32-bit keys), 24.67 vs 10.53 (64-bit key/448-bit value), 79.94 vs 30.64 (string keys), i.e. 2.3-2.6x (derived from page data); erase existing 11.26 vs 7.79, 9.84 vs 6.10, 3.21 vs 2.41, i.e. 1.3-1.6x (derived from page data); erase nonexisting 5.25 vs 3.72, 5.83 vs 3.91, 2.43 vs 1.93, i.e. 1.3-1.5x (derived from page data); lookup nonexisting 3.67 vs 3.22, 3.96 vs 3.24, 2.32 vs 1.83, i.e. 1.1-1.3x (derived from page data); insert 64-bit/448-bit 4.91 vs 4.11 and string 2.87 vs 2.61 (1.1-1.2x, derived from page data); string-key lookup existing 1.59 vs 1.38 and replace 1.52 vs 1.46 (1.04-1.15x, derived from page data). uthash is NOT faster for 32-bit-key insert (6.75 vs 6.39), 32-bit and 64-bit/448-bit replace (3.80 vs 2.71, 2.90 vs 2.34), or 32-bit and 64-bit/448-bit lookup of existing keys (2.58 vs 2.28, 2.45 vs 2.41).

notes: All heatmap figures in the record were re-extracted from the SVG in docs/index.md and match; added the omitted string-key lookup/replace rows and the 64-bit/448-bit lookup-existing loss. Shortcomings: win over std::unordered_map is mixed and confined to the 0-20M run (the 0-200,000 CSV shows uthash slower for nearly all insert, lookup and replace cases, e.g. 32-bit lookup existing at N=200,000 35,300 vs 15,700), the article author calls uthash all-around poor and far behind open-addressing tables, benchmarked v2.3.0 (repo now v2.4.0), Windows/MinGW libstdc++ only, and std::unordered_map was run with max load factor 0.875 rather than its default 1.0. License BSD-1-Clause (single retention clause, OSI-approved), 4.8k stars, last commit 2026-06-25 confirmed.

tier_reason: Independent third-party table from the cmark (CommonMark reference) project's benchmarks.md lists discount 1.86 s vs Markdown.pl 2921.24 s on an 11 MB input with a public 'make bench' driver, but the CPU is only 'Intel Core 2 Duo at 2GHz' (no model) and Discount's version, compiler and flags are unstated, so it falls short of A.

corrections.caveats: The numbers come from the cmark project's own benchmarks.md (tag 0.18), measured on an old Core 2 Duo laptop, not from Discount's repo, which has no benchmark. Discount version, compiler and flags are not stated; the benchmark driver is the public 'make bench' target in the cmark Makefile (time -p with and without input, median of ten runs) and the input is built from the public progit/progit repository. The cmark 0.13 table gave discount 1.705 s on the same input; Discount stayed in the table (1.85 s) through cmark 0.29.0 and was dropped at 0.30.0, when the table was re-run on an i9 MacBook Pro with only commonmark.js, cmark and md4c. The Markdown.pl figure (2921.24 s) is identical in every table from 0.13 to 0.29.0, so it was apparently measured once and carried over rather than re-run beside each Discount timing. Markdown.pl is a regex-based Perl reference implementation, so beating it is a weak result; Discount is not the fastest C Markdown library (sundown 0.34 s and cmark 0.36 s are about 5x faster in the same table, and hoedown 0.21 s in later tables). The measured Discount is a 2014-era release; the repo is now at 3.0.2.0.

notes: Numbers match cmark 0.18 benchmarks.md exactly; corrected the caveat that later cmark releases dropped Discount (it stays through 0.29.0 at 1.85 s). Shortcomings: weak baseline (Markdown.pl), about 5x slower than sundown/cmark/hoedown in the same table, old unnamed Core 2 Duo, no compiler/flags/version, Markdown.pl number carried over across releases.
